In Damasio’s words, “Inevitably, emotions are inseparable from the idea of good and evil”.","paragraphIndex":20047,"printedPages":[360]}],"status":"whole_book_source_structured_classroom_notes","basis":"uploaded_textbook_pdf_and_markdown","evidenceMethod":"source_heading_facts","sourceFactCount":7,"editorialVerification":"source-aligned, individual paraphrase review pending","followUpExplanation":"For example, it supports the idea of that emotions occur along dimensions instead of distinct categories.","followUpParagraphIndex":20044}],"classroomParagraphs":["Researchers had long recognized that the sympathetic nervous system stimulates certain organs, such as the heart, while inhibiting others, such as the stomach and intestines.","Walter Cannon was the first to recognize the pattern: It stimulates organs important for vigorous “fight-or-flight” activities while inhibiting vegetative activities that can wait until later. The parasympathetic nervous system is the “rest and digest” system that saves energy and prepares for later needs.","If a small animal sees a potential predator at a great distance, it becomes alert, but motionless. (The predator is less likely to notice an immobile animal.) The little animal’s heart rate decreases, by increased parasympathetic input.","In people with a condition called pure autonomic failure, the autonomic nervous system completely or almost completely ceases activity.","The heart and other organs continue to function, but the nervous system no longer regulates them. They report “having” the same emotions as anyone else, and they have little difficulty identifying what emotion a character in a story would probably experience, but they feel their emotions less intensely than before.","Presumably, when they report experiencing emotions, they refer mainly to the cognitive aspect: “I’m angry, because this is a situation that calls for anger.” People with damage to the right somatosensory cortex have typical autonomic responses to emotional music but report little subjective experience.","It is easier to feel angry while standing (and therefore in a position to attack) than while lying in a more helpless position.","Because perceptions of your body’s actions contribute to your emotional feelings, psychologists describe emotions as “embodied”—that is, they depend on the body’s responses.","Researchers could not test this hypothesis simply by telling people to smile or frown and then asking how they felt.","To disguise their intention, they asked people to hold a pen with either the teeth or the lips. The first study reported that people holding a pen with their teeth were more likely to rate cartoons as being funny.","When people face a camera, they tend to think about how they look on the camera, and it changes their reactions.","A later study found that holding the pen in the teeth did increase amusement if no camera was Laboratory studies have found support for the facial feedback hypothesis that is reasonably dependable, although it is a small effect.","Another way to alter facial expressions is to use botulinum toxin (Botox), which blocks transmission at nerve– muscle junctions.","In the late 1800s and early 1900s, psychological researchers hoped to identify the elements of the mind, analogous to the elements of chemistry.","They debated whether the psychological elements were thoughts, ideas, images, or something else.","Later psychologists hoped to find the elements of motivation, offering lists of the basic motivations.","That pursuit led to such fascinating questions as whether breathing counts as just one motivation or two (inhaling and exhaling). Today, emotion is the only area in which many researchers still hope to identify the elements, the “basic” emotions.","The alternative is to regard emotional experience in terms of continuous dimensions.","Heart rate and breathing rate increase with the intensity of an emotion, but they do not distinguish fear from anger, or any other pair of emotions.","Traditionally, the limbic system — the forebrain areas surrounding the thalamus—has been regarded as important for emotion (Figure 11.3).","Researchers have used PET or fMRI techniques to identify brain areas that respond while people look at emotional pictures or listen to emotional stories.","The only emotion that seems to depend mostly on one brain area is disgust, which exhibits a link to the insula, a cortical area that is also important for taste. The researchers described the third gradient as “complexity,” ranging from conflict at one pole to unambiguous emotion (usually fearful) at the other.","In short, these findings support the idea that brain responses are well described as dimensions of emotion rather than as discrete categories.","Activity of the left hemisphere, especially its frontal and temporal lobes, relates to what Jeffrey Gray","called the behavioral activation system (BAS), marked by low to moderate autonomic arousal and a tendency to approach, which could characterize happiness or anger.","Activity of right hemisphere, again mainly the frontal and temporal lobes, is associated with the behavioral inhibition system (BIS). The BIS was initially described as responsible for withdrawal, but according to later research it is better described as inhibiting impulses and resolving conflict between drives.","People with greater right-hemisphere activity tend to be more socially withdrawn, cautious, and prone to unpleasant emotions.","The main support for the idea of basic emotions has relied on consistency of facial expressions.","People who are blind since birth exhibit expressions of happiness, sadness, fear, pride, and shame that resemble those of sighted people.","It is agreed that some emotional expressions are partly built-in, though capable of learned modification.","The controversial issue is whether those expressions fall into a small number of discrete categories. If presented with a set of faces, such as those in Figure 11.6, and given a list of emotion terms, most people in cultures throughout the world pair them up with greater-than-chance accuracy.","The procedure of asking people to match the six faces to six labels exaggerates the accuracy.","The procedure requires use of those six labels, even if an observer would have used some other label.","Finally, even if it were true that people could identify six emotions from facial expressions, that evidence would not demonstrate that we have precisely six emotions. Previous research had found disruptions in that axon tract in several psychiatric conditions marked by poor social relationships.","In short, details of brain anatomy have much to do with the ability to recognize emotional expressions.","If we evolved the capacity to experience and express emotions, emotions must have served some adaptive function.","Disgust tells us to avoid something that might cause illness. The adaptive value of happiness, sadness, embarrassment, and other emotions is more speculative, although psychologists have suggested plausible possibilities.","Research has also found that emotions provide a useful guide when we need to make a quick decision.","When we make important decisions, we pay much attention to how we think an outcome will make us feel.","However, although that may be true logically, the decisions","Brain scans demonstrate that contemplating these dilemmas activates brain areas known to respond to emotions, including parts of the prefrontal cortex and cingulate gyrus. People with the strongest autonomic arousal are the least likely to decide to kill one to save five others.","People with such damage tend to make decisions without much consideration of the emotional impact.","When confronted with the moral dilemmas we just discussed, they are more likely than average to choose the utilitarian option of killing one to save five. Almost everyone shudders and says of course not, but some people with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex calmly say it would be okay to do so.","Biological research sheds light on important questions about the psychology of emotions.","For example, it supports the idea of that emotions occur along dimensions instead of distinct categories.","Brain damage studies suggest that emotional reactions are often a useful quick guide to appropriate moral actions. Some people with ventromedial prefrontal cortex damage say yes, especially if the damage occurred early in life.","During the next few months, he exhibited impulsive behavior and poor decision making, two common symptoms of prefrontal damage.","Any choice requires consideration of values and emotions—how we think one outcome or another will make us feel. In Damasio’s words, “Inevitably, emotions are inseparable from the idea of good and evil”."],"classroomResearch":{"title":"Evidence in context: Actions Alter Emotions","body":"A later study found that holding the pen in the teeth did increase amusement if no camera was","printedPages":[354],"pdfPages":[372],"kind":"textbook_selected_research","evidenceMethod":"single_verified_textbook_passage"},"classroomCoverage":{"status":"source_structured_full_book","level":"comprehensive_book_derived","topicHeadings":10,"bullets":31,"newWords":1260,"allTopicsWithExplanations":true,"sourceScope":"verified_pdf_topic_facts_crosschecked_with_uploaded_markdown"}},{"id":"bp14-m11-2","chapterId":"bp14-ch11","moduleId":"bp14-m11-2","moduleNumber":"11.2","title":"Attack and Escape Behaviors","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":363,"printedEnd":375,"pdfStart":381,"pdfEnd":393,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Attack, escape, fear, and anxiety involve interacting biological systems rather than a single cause. Genetic and environmental influences, hormones, serotonin, and amygdala function all figure in the evidence."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The module also examines anxiety disorders and methods of relief. Compare evidence from animals and humans while paying attention to the limits of applying one experimental finding to complex human behavior."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-2-study-1","text":"Aggression has many causes"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Attack behavior varies substantially across species and situations. Genetic background, learning, environmental circumstances, hormones, and neural systems can influence its probability. Testosterone is often discussed, but a simple equation of testosterone with violence is inadequate. Serotonin-related mechanisms have also been studied in aggression, yet their effects depend on circuits, receptors, and context. The same individual may respond differently when threatened, competing, or in a familiar social environment."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-2-study-2","text":"Fear and the amygdala"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amygdala participates in detecting and learning about biologically important cues, especially threats in many studied tasks. Experiments in rodents, monkeys, and humans reveal overlapping and differing roles. Damage can alter reactions to threatening information, but the amygdala is not a magical switch that contains every experience of fear. Visual stimuli, other sensory cues, learning history, and frontal regulation all influence a response. Different research methods reveal different parts of this wider system."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-2-study-3","text":"Anxiety is not identical to fear"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Fear typically refers to a response to a more immediate threat, whereas anxiety often concerns anticipation or uncertainty about potential danger. These states can overlap and recruit related neural systems. Anxiety disorders involve patterns of distress and impairment rather than simply ordinary nervousness. Individual differences in amygdala reactivity and other measures can correlate with anxiety, but such correlations are not a diagnostic test or a complete explanation of a person's symptoms."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-2-study-4","text":"Ways of reducing anxiety"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Pharmacological approaches can alter relevant neural signaling, while behavioral or cognitive approaches may change learned responses and coping. Alcohol can temporarily influence anxiety but brings significant risks and is not a reliable solution. Treatment is best understood through benefits, side effects, and patterns of evidence rather than as an attempt to 'turn off the amygdala.' Across this module, distinguish attacks, fear responses, sustained anxiety, and the factors that make each more or less likely."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h01","text":"Attack Behaviors"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Attack behavior depends on the individual as well as the situation.","sourcePrintedPage":363,"sourcePdfPage":381,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If a hamster intrudes into another hamster’s territory, the home hamster sniffs the intruder and eventually attacks, but usually not at once.","sourcePrintedPage":363,"sourcePdfPage":381,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The first attack enhances home hamster’s readiness to attack against any intruder for the next 30 minutes or more .","sourcePrintedPage":363,"sourcePdfPage":381,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is as if the first attack gets the hamster in the mood to fight.","sourcePrintedPage":363,"sourcePdfPage":381,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"During that period, activity builds up in the corticomedial area of the amygdala (Figure 11.10), and as it does so, it increases the hamster’s probability of attacking .","sourcePrintedPage":363,"sourcePdfPage":381,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some people have argued that it is “in our animal nature” to be violent, at least for males.","sourcePrintedPage":363,"sourcePdfPage":381,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"troops are extremely, even murderously aggressive, but chimps in other troops are much less aggressive, and bonobos rarely fight at all .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People are capable of unspeakable cruelty, but cooperative behavior is vastly more common .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h02","text":"Genetic and Environmental Influences"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Twin studies generally indicate significant heritability, but the results vary for many reasons, including how the researchers measure aggression .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A study of prisoners with a history of extreme impulsive violence found that 123 of the 281 men studied had one or more rare genetic variants linked to brain functioning .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Of the rare genetic variants linked to a high probability of violence, the one most thoroughly studied is a gene causing deficiency of monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After a neuron releases serotonin, dopamine, or norepinephrine, most of it returns to the neuron via reuptake.","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A deficiency MAOA increases the build-up of serotonin inside neurons, evidently altering early brain development in a way that increases the risk of antisocial behavior, especially in males .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the MAOA gene is on the X chromosome, males are far more likely than females to have the variant form of the gene without a normal form to compete with it.","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Research with mice also demonstrates a link between a genetic deficiency of MAOA and later aggressive behavior .","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This result is fascinating because of its apparent demonstration of an interaction between genetics and environment.","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h03","text":"Testosterone"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most fighting in the animal kingdom is by males competing for mates, and their aggressive behavior depends on testosterone.","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The natural assumption is that testosterone increases violent behavior, and yet, for humans the evidence is","sourcePrintedPage":364,"sourcePdfPage":382,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In those cases, the correlation between baseline testosterone level and aggressive behavior is statistically significant (if we study a large enough group), but low (less than 0.1).","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amount that testosterone increases in an emotional situation correlates a little higher with aggression, but still less than 0.2 .","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because females start with low testosterone levels, an increase might produce more effect than it does in males.","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In one study, testosterone increased the amount of time females spent looking at angry faces .","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This result fits with other research finding that committees work more harmoniously if they include a high percentage of females—of course, females who hadn’t just been given testosterone .","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h04","text":"Serotonin Synapses and Aggressive Behavior"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Several lines of evidence link impulsive, aggressive behavior to low serotonin release.","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Luigi Valzelli found that isolating male mice for 4 weeks increased their aggressive behavior and decreased their serotonin turnover , the amount that neurons released and replaced.","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When neurons release serotonin, they reabsorb most of it and synthesize enough to replace the amount that washed away.","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers measure serotonin turnover by the concentration of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) , serotonin’s main metabolite, in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One reason is that some studies measured actual behavior, whereas others relied on answers to questionnaires .","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Also, many studies relied on serotonin measurements from the blood, which correlates poorly with serotonin in the brain .","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Overall, low serotonin turnover does appear to correlate with human aggressive behavior, but not strongly.","sourcePrintedPage":365,"sourcePdfPage":383,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cortisol increases during anxiety and decreases during anger .","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A study of adolescents found aggressive behavior correlated with high levels of testosterone and low levels of cortisol in their hair .","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This type of behavior is a long way from serious violence, and maybe that is why most experiments find only weak relationships to testosterone or other chemicals.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h05","text":"Fear and Anxiety"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Yes, at least one: A sudden loud noise causes newborns to arch their backs, briefly extend their arms and legs, and cry.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Whether to call this behavior fear is a matter of opinion. (The alternative is “distress.”) After infancy, a loud noise elicits the closely related startle reflex : Auditory information from the cochlear nucleus in the medulla goes directly to an area in the pons that tenses the muscles, especially the neck muscles.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Tensing the neck muscles is important because the neck is so vulnerable to injury.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although you don’t have to learn to fear loud noises, your current mood or situation modifies your reaction.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"So do people who report much anxiety, even if they don’t qualify for a psychiatric diagnosis .","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The suitability of the startle reflex to measure anxiety means that we can use it with not only with humans, but also with laboratory animals to explore the brain mechanisms.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h06","text":"Role of the Amygdala in Rodents"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Extensive research with rodents has demonstrated the importance of the amygdala for fear and anxiety.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The brain pathways are the same in humans , but the research can go into more detail with rodents.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In research with rodents, psychologists first measure the startle response to a sudden loud noise.","sourcePrintedPage":366,"sourcePdfPage":384,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Conversely, a stimulus previously associated with something pleasant, or with the absence of danger, becomes a safety signal that decreases the startle reflex .","sourcePrintedPage":367,"sourcePdfPage":385,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Investigators determined that the amygdala (Figures 11.10 and 11.13) is important for modifying the startle reflex, and for learned fears in general.","sourcePrintedPage":367,"sourcePdfPage":385,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An odd parasite has evolved a way to exploit the consequences of amygdala damage .","sourcePrintedPage":367,"sourcePdfPage":385,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan that infects many mammals but reproduces only in cats.","sourcePrintedPage":367,"sourcePdfPage":385,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the parasite enters a rodent, in many cases (about 50 percent) it migrates to the brain where it damages the amygdala.","sourcePrintedPage":367,"sourcePdfPage":385,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amygdala is important for learning to fear a particular stimulus, but that is not the only type of fear.","sourcePrintedPage":367,"sourcePdfPage":385,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"I need to be alert for threats.” This long-term, generalized emotional arousal depends on a brain area called the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis .","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h07","text":"Studies in Monkeys"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The effect of amygdala damage in monkeys was first described in classic studies early in the 1900s and is known as the Klüver-Bucy syndrome, from the names of the primary investigators.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Monkeys with this syndrome are tame and placid.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They attempt to pick up lighted matches and other objects that they ordinarily avoid.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They display less than the normal fear of snakes or dominant monkeys .","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They have impaired social behaviors, largely because they don’t seem to learn which monkeys to approach with caution.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Like rats with amygdala damage, monkeys with such damage are impaired at learning what to fear .","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h08","text":"Response of the Human Amygdala to Visual Stimuli"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Studies with fMRI find that the human amygdala responds strongly when people look at photos that arouse fear or at photos of faces expressing fear or anger .","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amygdala can also respond to pleasant stimuli if a task requires attention to pleasant stimuli, but even then, the response is never as great as it is to unpleasant stimuli .","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amygdala’s response to a frightened face emerges in the remarkably fast time of just 74 milliseconds (ms) after presentation of the photo , faster than the response by the fusiform gyrus and other areas responsible for facial recognition.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"You respond to the fear in someone’s face before you recognize whose face it is.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Contrary to what we might guess, the amygdala responds most strongly when a facial expression is difficult to interpret.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is usually easy to interpret an angry face looking straight at you, but a fearful face looking straight at you can be puzzling.","sourcePrintedPage":368,"sourcePdfPage":386,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-2-h09","text":"Damage to the Human Amygdala"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"With laboratory animals, researchers can intentionally damage the amygdala to see the effects.","sourcePrintedPage":369,"sourcePdfPage":387,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When people experience a stroke that damages the amygdala and surrounding areas, at least in one hemisphere, they are impaired in certain ways.","sourcePrintedPage":369,"sourcePdfPage":387,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They can
